Title: First-Order Primal-Dual Repairs for Scalable Branch and Bound
Authors: Francesco Pivi, Jiachang Liu, Andrea Lodi
Affiliations: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology
Abstract: Mixed-integer programs have found applications in many real-world problems but remain difficult to solve at scale. To improve scalability, there has been increasing interest in incorporating first-order methods as subroutines for solving node relaxations, with success primarily on problems involving specific types of constraints. However, when more general constraints are considered, first-order methods cannot be directly applied because, at finite iterations, they typically produce infeasible primal and dual solutions, preventing their direct integration into branch-and-bound. To overcome this limitation, we introduce repair procedures that extract valid primal and dual bounds from infeasible first-order iterates. These bounds enable node pruning, incumbent updates, and early stopping at any iteration. Empirically, our approach achieves one to two orders of magnitude speedups when solving real-world instances (with another order of magnitude speedup when running on GPUs) and certifies optimality on instances that are difficult for commercial solvers.

Title: Observing the unobserved confounding through its effects: toward randomized trial-like estimates from real-world survival data
Authors: Vasiliki Stoumpou, Dimitris Bertsimas, Samuel Singer, Georgios Antonios Margonis
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Abstract: Background: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are costly, time-consuming, and often infeasible, while treatment-effect estimation from observational data is limited by unobserved confounding. Methods: We developed a three-step framework to address unobserved confounding in observational survival data. First, we infer a latent prognostic factor (U) from restricted mean survival time (RMST) discrepancies between patients with similar observed factors, the same treatment, and divergent outcomes, leveraging the idea that the aggregate effect of unmeasured factors can be inferred even if individual factors cannot. Second, we balance U with observed baseline covariates using prognostic matching, entropy balancing, or inverse probability of treatment weighting. Third, we apply multivariable survival analysis to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). We evaluated the framework in three observational cohorts with RCT benchmarks, two RCT cohorts, and six multicenter observational cohorts. Results: In three observational cohorts (nine comparisons), balancing U improved agreement with trial HRs in all cases; in the strongest settings, it reduced absolute log-HR error by approximately ten-fold versus using observed covariates alone (mean reduction 0.344; p=0.001). In two RCT cohorts, U was balanced across arms (most SMDs <0.1) and adjustment had minimal impact on log-HRs (mean absolute change 0.08). Across six multicenter cohorts, balancing U within centers reduced cross-center dispersion in chemotherapy log-HR estimates (mean reduction 0.147; p=0.016); when populations were directly balanced across centers to account for case-mix differences, cross-center survival differences were narrowed in 75%-100% of comparisons. Conclusions: Inferring and balancing a latent prognostic signal may reduce unobserved confounding and improve treatment-effect estimation from real-world data.

Title: Robustifying and Selecting Cohort-Appropriate Prognostic Models under Distributional Shifts
Authors: Dimitris Bertsimas, Carol Gao, Angelos Georgios Koulouras, Georgios Antonios Margonis
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Abstract: External validation is widely regarded as the gold standard for prognostic model evaluation. In this study, we challenge the assumption that successful external calibration guarantees model generalizability and propose two complementary strategies to improve transportability of prognostic models across cohorts. Using six real-world surgical cohorts from tertiary academic centers, we tested whether successful external calibration depends largely on similarity in covariates and outcomes between training and validation cohorts, quantified using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, with calibration assessed by the Integrated Calibration Index (ICI). From the model-developer's perspective, we trained the "best-on-average" prognostic model by tuning toward a meta-analysis-derived covariate and outcome distribution as an approximation of the broader target population. From the end-user perspective, we proposed a simple measure for cohort outcome similarity to identify, among published models, the one most suitable for a given target cohort in terms of both calibration and clinical utility. External calibration worsened as distributional mismatch increased. Higher KL divergence was associated with higher ICI in both surgery-alone (Spearman $ρ=0.614$, $p=0.004$) and surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy cohorts (Spearman $ρ=0.738$, $p<0.001$). Meta-analysis-informed weighting improved calibration in most settings without materially affecting discrimination, with the clearest benefit when evaluated on the aggregated external population ($p=0.037$). Models developed in more similar cohorts achieved lower ICI in surgery-alone (Spearman $ρ=0.803$, $p<0.001$) and surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy cohorts (Spearman $ρ=0.737$, $p<0.001$), and provided greater clinical utility on DCA.

Title: A Multimodal and Explainable Machine Learning Approach to Diagnosing Multi-Class Ejection Fraction from Electrocardiograms
Authors: Catherine Ning, Yu Ma, Cindy Wang, Sean McMahon, Joseph A. Radojevic, STEVEN L. ZWEIBEL, Dimitris Bertsimas
Affiliations: University of Wisconsin–Madison; Hartford Hospital
Abstract: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) assessment depends on echocardiography, limiting access in primary care and resource-constrained settings. We developed a multimodal machine-learning framework that combines engineered 12-lead ECG timeseries features with structured EHR variables to classify LVEF into four clinically used strata: normal (>50%), mildly reduced (40-50%), moderately reduced (30-40%), and severely reduced (<30%). To support model explainability, we identified the most influential ECG and EHR features via SHAP attributions. Using retrospective data from Hartford HealthCare, we trained XGBoost models on 36,784 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from 30,952 outpatients and evaluated temporal generalizability on 19,966 ECGs from a subsequent period. The multimodal model achieved one-vs-rest AUROCs of 0.95 (severe), 0.92 (moderate), 0.82 (mild), and 0.91 (normal), outperforming ECG-only and EHR-only baselines, and maintained performance under temporal validation. This work supports ECG-based, multimodal LVEF stratification as a practical screening and triage aid to prioritize confirmatory imaging where resources are limited.

Title: Bespoke: Generating MOOC-Quality Industry-Personalized Lecture Videos at Scale
Authors: Romain Puech, Dewang Kumar Agarwal, Antonio Santamaría Escobar, Dimitris Bertsimas
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Lifelong learners from different industries often watch the same recorded lecture, even when they will apply the material in different workplaces. We present Bespoke, a system that takes the transcript of an existing lecture and generates a new video customized to a target industry and duration, with new slides, narration, and charts. From 31 graduate lectures in analytics, machine learning, and optimization, we generated 209 videos for these three industries, plus a generic-audience version of each lecture. Twenty-five experts in the corresponding domains rated 92 videos on a five-point rubric. They judged 87% at or above the rubric midpoint corresponding to ``a standard MOOC lecture's quality'' (mean overall score 3.42 out of 5; 48% scored 4 or above). Overall quality was similar across industries, durations, and a 21-lecture held-out set unused while developing the system, at about \$0.22 API cost per minute of video.

Title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
Authors: Romain Puech, Georgy Salakhutdinov, Dimitris Bertsimas
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.

Title: Decision-Weighted Limit Theorems: Less Conservative Robust Optimization
Authors: Dimitris Bertsimas, Danique de Moor, Dick van Hertog, Federica Donnini
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; University of Florence
Abstract: Limit theorems provide a natural way to construct tractable models for optimization under uncertainty. Existing approaches typically apply them to unweighted sums of uncertain parameters and use the resulting bounds to construct uncertainty sets. We show that sharper formulations are obtained by applying limit theorems directly to the uncertain linear expressions in the optimization problem, with the decision variables as weights. For independent random variables with finite variance, the weighted central limit theorem yields a second-order cone constraint with a decision-dependent protection term, and for heavy-tailed random variables governed by stable limit laws, the weighted approach yields power-cone constraints. Using norm duality, we show that, under a condition on the individual bounds, the feasible region of the unweighted formulation is contained in that of the weighted one. In 16,000 knapsack instances with a prescribed violation probability of 5%, the weighted formulation improves the optimal objective value by 20.9% on average, with overall average violation probabilities between 3.45% and 4.95%, whereas those of the unweighted formulation are near zero.

Title: Platform architecture determines whether recommendation algorithms can shape information quality on social media
Authors: Mohammad Hammas Saeed, David André Broniatowski, Joseph R. Simons, Erica Lynn Gralla, Manan Suri, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia
Affiliations: George Washington University; University of Maryland, College Park
Abstract: Social media platforms shape public discourse through two fundamental design choices that naturally co-occur in any field investigation: platform architecture, which defines what types of actors exist and how they interact, and recommendation algorithm, which determines what content is surfaced to users. Using agent-based simulation, we orthogonally manipulate both factors, exploring four prototypical architectures -- tree (e.g., Reddit), layered hierarchy (e.g., Facebook), network (e.g., Twitter), and complete graph (e.g., TikTok) -- and two algorithms: chronological (LIFO) and popularity-based (Hot). Drawing on prior theory that identifies and ranks canonical system architectures in terms of their flexibility we hypothesize that algorithmic effects on information spread and quality should be largest on the most flexible platforms and smallest on the most constrained ones. We find strong confirmation of this prediction. On tree-like platforms like Reddit, the algorithm has no detectable effect on information spread and quality. On layered hierarchies and networks like Facebook and Twitter, respectively, the Hot algorithm has modest positive effects on both the spread of information and its quality. On complete structures like TikTok, the Hot algorithm leads to a winner-take-all dynamics that has strong negative effects on both information spread and quality, making the relation between content quality and popularity unpredictable. These findings imply that architectural considerations are more powerful levers than algorithmic interventions for the design of healthy online spaces and public discourse. Platform reform efforts focused exclusively on algorithm choice may be insufficient on architecturally unconstrained platforms and unnecessary on architecturally constrained ones.

Title: Drive, Pack, Fly: The Travelling Thief Problem with Drone
Authors: Kabir Murjani, Abhay Sobhanan
Affiliations: Nirma University; Indian Institute of Management Bangalore
Abstract: In collection operations, accumulating payload progressively slows the vehicle, imposing a cumulative penalty on routing efficiency. An onboard drone can offset this penalty by retrieving outlying items, thereby shortening the makespan and increasing operational profit. However, travel time remains load-dependent, and each item collected by the ground vehicle shifts the arrival times that govern the drone's launch and rendezvous points. This paper introduces the Travelling Thief Problem with Drone (TTP-D), which maximises the collected profit, net of a time-based rental cost, by jointly optimising item selection, vehicle routing, and flight synchronisation. We formulate a mixed-integer linear program that solves small instances to optimality, and develop both metaheuristics and an attention-based Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) policy for larger instances. We further propose a learner-initialised hybrid solver, in which the DRL policy constructs an initial solution that a short annealing run subsequently refines. On two benchmark sets, this hybrid recovers most of the metaheuristic baseline's quality at a fraction of its computational budget, although the largest instances still require the baseline at its full budget. Finally, a sensitivity analysis reveals that the rental ratio is the primary driver of profitability, whereas the fleet parameters affect profit only at the margin.

Title: Tight Guarantees for Static Policies in Vehicle Sharing Networks
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Jiaqi Shi
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: We study pricing in a vehicle sharing network with $N$ locations and $C$ vehicles, motivated by on-demand bike, scooter, and car sharing, as well as robotaxi and ride sharing services. Customers request directed trips between locations, with travel times following general distributions, and leave without service if no vehicle is available. Pricing affects both demand for trips and the distribution of vehicles across locations. Computing an optimal dynamic pricing policy is challenging because the system state depends on the number of vehicles available at each location and in transit (including how long they have been traveling), motivating the use of simple static policies that offer a fixed price for each trip. For any number of vehicles and locations, we establish a tight performance guarantee for static pricing relative to optimal dynamic pricing. The guarantee holds for any concave objective functions (including revenue rate) and general travel time distributions. Our tight guarantee is bounded below by $ \frac{C}{C + \min \{ C -1, \sqrt{ CN} \} }$ (over 50%), achieving the first universal, non-asymptotic constant factor guarantee. We also prove that the optimal static policy can be efficiently computed by solving a convex optimization problem. Finally, we extend our performance guarantee to the setting with supply redirection.

Title: Settling the Approximability of Submodular Facility Location
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Bento Natura, Meike Neuwohner
Affiliations: Columbia University; Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
Abstract: In submodular facility location (SFL), introduced by Svitkina and Tardos (SODA 2006), clients $\mathcal{C}$ in a metric space are assigned to facilities $\mathcal{F}$. A facility serving a set $S \subseteq \cal C$ of clients incurs cost $g(S)$, where $g$ is a monotone submodular function common to all facilities. The best known approximation factor for SFL is $O(\log\log|\mathcal{C}|)$, due to Abbasi, Adamczyk, Bosch-Calvo, Byrka, Grandoni, Sornat, and Tinguely (ICALP 2024), improving on the $O(\log|\mathcal{C}|)$-approximation of Svitkina and Tardos. We show that this is best possible up to a constant factor in the value-oracle model by showing that there exists no algorithm with only polynomially many queries to $g$ with approximation ratio $o(\log\log|\mathcal{C}|)$. This bound holds for algorithms with unlimited computation time, and when $g$ is restricted to matroid rank functions. We also show that the natural linear programming relaxation has an integrality gap of $Θ(\log\log|\mathcal{C}|)$. Our lower bound follows by constructing an extension of Vondrák's symmetry-gap approach (FOCS 2009) for matroid rank functions.

Title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Tianyi Lin, Wenxuan Liu
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.

Title: Joint Service Depth and Priority Design in Queueing Systems
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Yash Kanoria, Jonathan Y. Tan
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: In AI-assisted service systems, the server can choose how much processing effort to spend on each job, which we call the service depth. Deeper reasoning improves output quality but occupies the server longer and increases congestion, and the realized processing time remains random because AI models are probabilistic and tasks vary in complexity. We study the joint design of service depth and priority in a single-server queue whose customers differ in delay sensitivity, with the goal of maximizing social welfare. For each customer type, the decision maker chooses a priority level and a service depth, and service times are exponential with mean equal to the chosen depth. With two customer types and linear service values, we characterize the centralized optimum. Counterintuitively, it prioritizes the patient type and gives it a smaller service depth when patient customers are sufficiently prevalent. When delay sensitivity is private, however, incentive compatibility requires the impatient type to receive a weakly shorter sojourn time, so the optimal price menu never prioritizes the patient type. Consequently, there can be a welfare gap between the centralized decision maker's optimal control policy and the optimal decentralized pricing mechanism. With a continuum of types, the centralized optimum is monotone: more delay-sensitive customers receive weakly smaller depth and higher priority, so the optimum can be implemented by a price menu with no welfare loss. Allowing randomized depths similarly closes the gap in the two-type model. Finally, we calibrate an agentic AI service system using published coding-agent trials from DeepSWE and numerically examine priority inversion, the value of joint design, and the welfare gain from personalization.

Title: Commodity Carry and Long-Run Inventory Risk

Title: Rule-Based Pricing Algorithms and Market Outcomes: An Experimental Study
Authors: Adrian Hillenbrand, Hans‐Theo Normann, Matthias Potarca, Tobias Werner
Affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology; Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf; National University of Ireland, Maynooth
Abstract: Rule-based pricing tools are widespread in digital commerce, yet we know little about how their design shapes market outcomes. In a controlled market experiment, participants use dashboards to build pricing algorithms competing in a sequential Bertrand game over multiple periods. We vary design features commonly found in commercial repricing tools: warnings about price wars, pre-configured strategies, and advice from a large language model. Most treatment variations raise market prices with effects driven by an increase in starting prices and more cooperative algorithm designs. The results matter for competition policy, platform regulation and current discussions on regulating algorithm design tools.

Title: No Certificate, No Execution: Certified Traces as a Foundation for Trustworthy AI Agents
Authors: Xiao-Yang Liu Yanglet, Xiaodong Wang, Agostino Capponi
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: We argue that trustworthy AI agents, especially in high-stakes and policy-governed domains, should make execution conditional on certified traces rather than rely only on stronger generative models, output-level guardrails, or post-hoc audits. A generative agent may propose recommendations, tool calls, reports, or actions, but generation is not permission: an action may be computable yet impermissible, and individually permissible actions may compose into an impermissible trace. We formalize trustworthy agency through a \textbf{Proposal--Certification--Execution (PCE)} architecture: a probabilistic generating machine $M_G$ proposes candidate execution traces, a \textbf{Permissibility Machine} $M_Π$ certifies proposed traces under a policy system $Π$, and execution proceeds only for certified traces. The executable trace language is $L_{\mathrm{exec}} = L_G \cap L_{\mathrm{cert}}(M_Π)$. Before execution, a trace is a structured pre-execution record submitted for certification: it specifies intended steps, evidence, proposed tool calls, approvals, replayable computations, credentials, and execution conditions. This perspective complements chain-of-thought monitorability: visible reasoning may help detect misbehavior, but monitorability is not certifiability, and reasoning is only one component of a broader execution trace. The formal principle is simple: an agent-generated trace should execute only when it carries a checkable certificate witnessing permissibility under $Π$: \textbf{no certificate, no execution}. We develop certified traces and Permissibility Machines as foundations for trustworthy AI agents, connect trace certification to proof-carrying execution, proof memory, privacy, and zero-knowledge certificates, and propose evaluating agents by what generated traces can be safely certified for execution, not by output accuracy alone.

Title: SmartEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Generated Smart Contracts from Natural Language Specifications
Authors: Abhinav Goel, Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo, Chaitya Shah
Affiliations: Columbia University; IBM (United States)
Abstract: We introduce SmartEval, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the quality of Solidity smart contracts generated by large language models (LLMs) from natural language specifications. SmartEval provides a corpus of 9,000 generated contracts paired with expert-written ground-truth implementations drawn from the FSMSCG dataset, a five-dimensional evaluation rubric covering functional completeness, variable fidelity, state-machine correctness, business-logic fidelity, and code quality, and a reproducible generation-and-evaluation pipeline. To validate the benchmark's reliability, we conduct three independent empirical studies: a five-condition ablation study (N=300 per condition) isolating the contribution of each pipeline component, a human expert evaluation by three Columbia University PhD researchers confirming automated scores align with expert judgment to within 0.34 points, and external security analysis via the Slither static analyzer confirming 79.4% agreement between the LLM auditor and a non-LLM rule-based tool. Systematic analysis of 9,000 generated contracts reveals characteristic failure modes (logic omissions at 35.3%, state transition errors at 23.4%, and complexity-driven degradation) and quantifies a +8.29 composite-score advantage of generated contracts over ground-truth implementations, attributable to LLMs' literal specification-following behavior. SmartEval establishes a reproducible, validated foundation for empirical research on LLM smart contract synthesis quality, with all data, evaluation code, and generated contracts publicly released.

Title: An end-to-end agentic pipeline for smart contract translation and quality evaluation
Authors: Abhinav Goel, Chaitya Shah, Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo
Affiliations: Columbia University; IBM (United States)
Abstract: We present an end-to-end framework for systematic evaluation of LLM-generated smart contracts from natural-language specifications. The system parses contractual text into structured schemas, generates Solidity code, and performs automated quality assessment through compilation and security checks. Using CrewAI-style agent teams with iterative refinement, the pipeline produces structured artifacts with full provenance metadata. Quality is measured across five dimensions, including functional completeness, variable fidelity, state-machine correctness, business-logic fidelity, and code quality aggregated into composite scores. The framework supports paired evaluation against ground-truth implementations, quantifying alignment and identifying systematic error modes such as logic omissions and state transition inconsistencies. This provides a reproducible benchmark for empirical research on smart contract synthesis quality and supports extensions to formal verification and compliance checking.

Title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
Authors: Abhinav Goel, Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo, Chaitya Shah
Affiliations: Columbia University; IBM (United States)
Abstract: AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost. We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines. We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.

Title: DynaSPLIT: Strong tail-optimal scheduling for the M/G/n with heavy-tailed job sizes
Authors: Zhouzi Li, Mor Harchol‐Balter, Alan Andrew Scheller-Wolf
Affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract: We study the asymptotic response time tail in the M/G/n queue with heavy-tailed (regularly varying) job sizes. For this setting, strongly tail optimal policies are known only at lower load, where n-1 servers suffice for stability. At higher load, the tail optimal scheduling has been open. This paper presents DynaSPLIT, the first strongly tail optimal policy at high load. Together with prior work, this result shows that strong tail optimality is achievable across the entire stability region of the M/G/n with heavy-tailed job sizes.

Title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
Authors: Amirhossein Zohrehvand, Aldona Kapacinskaite
Affiliations: INSEAD
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has made it easier than ever to produce research outputs. Adding an agentic tool to a research team's work potentially extends the team's capabilities but calls for an active approach to organizing the research process. The pressing question, therefore, is how research teams should organize their work with this technology. We contend that the question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people working with machines keep control of projects with many contributors. We distill principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they can help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. With TRACE, we aim to join a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI. We contend that a simple enough and useful standard can contribute to harnessing AI capabilities, allowing teams to delegate parts of their work to AI, while also building trust within teams and the broader research community.

Title: Reducing SNAP Payment Errors at Lower Cost With AI: A Simulation Study
Authors: Alex Chohlas-Wood
Affiliations: New York University
Abstract: New federal legislation will require states with high payment error rates in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to pay a share of benefit costs, potentially costing some states over a billion dollars per year. These costs create substantial pressure to improve payment accuracy. One strategy to improve payment accuracy is preauthorization review, in which staff double-check applications and correct mistakes before benefits are issued. But limited staff capacity makes it important to target these reviews effectively. One leading targeting approach uses statistical risk models to prioritize cases likely to contain errors. Another novel approach uses AI to flag specific potential discrepancies for reviewers to check. For states under pressure to reduce error rates, it is unclear which approach-or combination of approaches-would reduce payment error rates most effectively. We compare these strategies through simulations using public SNAP quality control data. Under our main assumptions, risk-based review alone costs about seven times as much as combining AI flags with risk scores. This cost advantage persists across a wide range of plausible assumptions. Our findings suggest that AI-assisted preauthorization review could be a key tool to help states avoid substantial cost-sharing obligations.

Title: Granulation in Color: The Chromatic Stellar Flicker of LTT-9779 and WASP-121
Authors: William C. Waalkes, Н. М. Костогрыз, Valeriy Vasilyev, Rafael Luque, Alexander Shapiro, Jordi Blanco-Pozo, Ana Glidden, Jeff Valenti, Sami Solanki, Ignasi Ribas, Sara Seager, L. Gizon
Affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research; Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía; Center for Astrophysics Harvard & Smithsonian; Space Telescope Science Institute; Institute of Space Sciences; University of Toronto
Abstract: Granulation is a persistent feature of stars with outer convective layers and is the photospheric signature of near-surface convective energy transport. In disk-integrated observations, it produces stochastic brightness variations that contribute substantially to stellar variability on timescales of minutes to hours. High-precision, observations with JWST provide an opportunity to study the chromatic signatures of stellar granulation. This work aims to measure the amplitude and characteristic timescale of granulation-induced variability for solar-type stars and to investigate whether the granulation signal shows significant chromatic variation in the near-infrared. We accessed publicly available JWST/NIRISS SOSS time-series observations of LTT-9779 (G7V) and WASP-121 (F6V) and de-trended the light curves by fitting the transits, eclipses, and planetary phase curves. We computed power spectra from the de-trended light curves and fit them with a Harvey granulation profile. We first analyzed the broadband light curves to measure and fix the granulation timescale and then repeated the power-spectrum analysis in individual wavelength channels to measure the chromatic dependence of the granulation amplitude. For LTT-9779, we measure a broadband granulation amplitude of σ$=53.8^{+4.1}_{-4.0}$ppm at a timescale of τ$=4.8^{+1.5}_{-1.3}$min. For WASP-121, we measure σ$=59.3\pm4.3$ppm and τ$=6.3^{+2.1}_{-1.8}$min. We also measure peak oscillation frequencies of ν$=3382^{+166}_{-191}μ$Hz and $1649^{+55}_{-69}μ$Hz in the bandpass-integrated power spectra of LTT-9779 and WASP-121, respectively. In the spectroscopic fits, we find $σ$ decreases with wavelength. Our results demonstrate a new observational window on short-timescale stellar variability and provides a way to characterize chromatic stellar noise in transit light curves.

Title: Statistical robustness and time consistency in risk averse optimization
Authors: Alexander Shapiro, Yan Li
Affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology; Texas A&M University
Abstract: The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.

Title: Let's Have a Conversation: Designing and Evaluating LLM Agents for Interactive Optimization
Authors: Joshua Drossman, Alexandre Jacquillat, Sébastien Martin
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Northwestern University
Abstract: Optimization is as much about modeling the right problem as solving it. Identifying the right objectives, constraints, and trade-offs demands extensive interaction between researchers and stakeholders. Large language models can empower decision-makers with optimization capabilities through interactive optimization agents that can propose, interpret and refine solutions. However, it is fundamentally harder to evaluate a conversation-based interaction than traditional one-shot approaches. This paper proposes a scalable and replicable methodology for evaluating optimization agents through conversations. We build LLM-powered decision agents that role-play diverse stakeholders, each governed by an internal utility function but communicating like a real decision-maker. We generate thousands of conversations in a school scheduling case study. Results show that one-shot evaluation is severely limiting: the same optimization agent converges to much higher-quality solutions through conversations. Then, this paper uses this methodology to demonstrate that tailored optimization agents, endowed with domain-specific prompts and structured tools, can lead to significant improvements in solution quality in fewer interactions, as compared to general-purpose chatbots. These findings provide evidence of the benefits of emerging solutions at the AI-optimization interface to expand the reach of optimization technologies in practice. They also uncover the impact of operations research expertise to facilitate interactive deployments through the design of effective and reliable optimization agents.

Title: Predictive and Prescriptive AI toward Optimizing Wildfire Suppression
Authors: Léonard Boussioux, Alexandre Jacquillat, Ryne Reger, Jacob Wachspress
Affiliations: University of Washington; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Intense wildfire seasons require critical prioritization decisions to allocate scarce suppression resources over a dispersed geographical area. This paper develops a predictive and prescriptive approach to jointly optimize crew assignments and wildfire suppression. The problem features a discrete resource-allocation structure with endogenous wildfire demand and non-linear wildfire dynamics. We formulate an integer optimization model with crew assignments on a time-space-rest network, wildfire dynamics on a time-state network, and linking constraints between them. We develop a two-sided branch-and-price-and-cut algorithm based on: (i) a two-sided column generation scheme that generates fire suppression plans and crew routes iteratively; (ii) a new family of cuts exploiting the knapsack structure of the linking constraints; and (iii) novel branching rules to accommodate non-linear wildfire dynamics. We also propose a data-driven double machine learning approach to estimate wildfire spread as a function of covariate information and suppression efforts, mitigating observed confounding between historical crew assignments and wildfire growth. Extensive computational experiments show that the optimization algorithm scales to otherwise intractable real-world instances; and that the methodology can enhance suppression effectiveness in practice, resulting in significant reductions in area burned over a wildfire season and guiding resource sharing across wildfire jurisdictions.

Title: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes: Modeling the Interplay of Skill, Effort, and AI Assistance
Authors: Ali Aouad, Thodoris Lykouris, Huiying Zhong
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly adopted in the workplace and in education, yet the empirical evidence on AI's impact remains mixed across different operating contexts. We propose a model of human-AI interaction to better understand and analyze several mechanisms by which AI affects productivity. In our setting, human agents with varying skill levels exert utility-maximizing effort to produce certain task outcomes with AI assistance. We find that incorporating endogeneity in skill development or AI unreliability can induce a productivity paradox: increased levels of AI assistance may degrade productivity, leading to potentially significant shortfalls. We construct interpretable measures that characterize when the productivity paradox occurs. Moreover, we examine the long-term distributional effect of AI on skill, and demonstrate that skill polarization can emerge in steady state. We identify an effort-skill non-monotonicity condition under which skill polarization emerges.

Title: Bayesian Optimal Stopping: Invincible Prophets and Achievable Philosophers
Authors: Alireza Amanihamedani, Ali Aouad, Senem Işık, Thomas Keßelheim, Amin Saberi
Abstract: We study Bayesian optimal stopping: a hidden world $H$ is drawn from $K$ worlds according to a known prior and determines the joint distribution of $n$ observations. A decision-maker selects one observation irrevocably to maximize its value, learning about the world as observations arrive. We compare algorithms against the Bayes-optimal online policy (the philosopher) and the offline optimum (the prophet). Our results show that the philosopher is achievable in that we find a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of the Bayes-optimal policy that runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal{I}|^{\log^* |\mathcal{I}| + 1/\varepsilon} \cdot (1/\varepsilon)^{1/\varepsilon^2})$, where $|\mathcal{I}|$ is the size of the input. By contrast, the prophet is invincible and no algorithm can obtain a competitive ratio that substantially exceeds the worst-case guarantees. When the observations are conditionally independent and identically distributed given $H$, the secretary's rule is $1/e$-competitive. We show that no algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio better than $1/e + 1/\mathrm{poly}(K)$ and this bound is attainable. Our approximation scheme builds on a primal improvement subroutine connecting the two benchmarks. Given an $α$-competitive algorithm against the prophet, we construct an algorithm with a strictly better approximation factor against the philosopher. We randomize between the baseline algorithm and a threshold algorithm based on dual martingales that exploit the Bayesian structure. Each improvement yields a tighter dual martingale, enabling repeated primal-dual updates. We approximate these martingales in polynomial time using importance-weighted Monte Carlo sampling. Dual martingales also establish our upper bound on the competitive ratio and may be useful for more general Bayesian online optimization problems.

Title: Conformal Predictive Distributions for Contextual Order Fulfillment Optimization
Authors: Tinghan Ye, Amira Hijazi, Pascal Van Hentenryck
Affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology
Abstract: Ship-to-home fulfillment requires a retailer to select a fulfillment location and carrier before the delivery time is known. These decisions often rely on static transit-time estimates, which cannot represent how delivery-time uncertainty varies across orders and fulfillment options. This paper constructs conformal predictive distributions (CPDs) using Conformal Predictive Systems (CPS) for regression and the cross Venn-Abers predictor (CVAP) for multiclass classification, and uses them in a contextual optimization model for fulfillment decisions. The model is solved by contextual sample-average approximation (C-SAA). The regret of each fulfillment decision, its expected cost above that of the best decision, is bounded by forecast error, scenario-evaluation error, and the candidate-generation gap. The forecast term depends on how well calibration residuals or class probabilities represent the current order. On more than five million proprietary order records, CVAP raises exact-day accuracy from 49.5% for the rule-based estimate to 64.1%. Paired with a decision rule that selects a quantile weighting late errors more heavily, the split CPS (SCPS) gives a point estimate that raises late-delivery detection from 3.8% to 79.4%. Residual-based CPS distributions also meet or slightly exceed nominal interval-coverage targets. In decision experiments with a JD.com simulator over six test dates, C-SAA with CVAP lowers mean total cost by 7.1% and C-SAA with the Mondrian CPS (MCPS) lowers it by 6.7%, relative to C-SAA with the original nonconformal forecast. Both cut the late-delivery rate from 5.7% to below 4.0%.

Authors: Lukas Stock, Andreas Schrimpf

Abstract: We present PyVesta, an automatic data reduction software for fiber fed echelle spectrographs. PyVesta is designed to be used with different instruments, both high resolution spectrographs such as HARPS or FEROS as well as inexpensive off-the-shelf spectrographs like the Shelyak eShel II. Special additions were implemented to improve the stability and resolution of inexpensive instruments especially. PyVesta provides tools for all extraction steps from raw CCD images to continuum normalized spectra, e.g., CCD image corrections, spectra extraction, wavelength calibration, and continuum normalization. Our software is based on the software package CERES and was ported to Python 3, revised, and supplemented.

Title: Moment Ambiguity and the Limits of Robust Stochastic Optimization
Authors: Andrés Cristi, Matteo Russo, J. Zhang
Abstract: We study fundamental information-theoretic limits of robust stochastic optimization when the distribution is known only through its exact moment sequence. We develop a unified framework that produces families of distinct distributions sharing all moments yet inducing radically different optimal decisions, thereby establishing strong impossibility results for a range of decision problems under moment ambiguity. Our binary and $N$-way moment-matching constructions separate quantiles, threshold regions, and online selection opportunities while preserving every moment. For the newsvendor problem, moment equivalence causes quantile ambiguity, inducing any fixed or randomized order quantity to fail arbitrarily badly. For revenue maximization, no deterministic or randomized posted pricing scheme can secure a nontrivial approximation relative to the full-information benchmark. For the secretary problem with cardinal observations, the optimal robust success probability under exact moment disclosure is the classical finite-horizon value $s_m$, even for i.i.d. observations. This value converges to $1/e$, compared with the full-information limit of approximately $0.5801$ due to Gilbert and Mosteller (J. Am. Stat. Assoc., 1966). We also recover and expand upon the recent impossibility result of Correa et al. (STOC, 2026) for prophet inequalities with moment knowledge. For every fixed $r\ge1$, exact moment knowledge can yield at best a $Θ(1/\log m)$ competitive ratio, even when competing against relaxed benchmarks based on expected $r$-th order statistics or when the algorithm is allowed to select $r$ items.

Title: The Pareto Secretary Problem
Authors: Andrés Cristi, Yilin Kong, J. Zhang
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne; Chinese University of Hong Kong
Abstract: The Pareto secretary problem asks for online selection of a Pareto-maximal observation from an i.i.d. sample: no other observation is at least as good in every coordinate and strictly better in one. For every fixed dimension $d\ge2$ and independent continuous coordinates, the optimal failure probability is of order $1/[(\log n)^{d-1}\log\log n]$, both with full information and with coordinate ranks alone. A deterministic rank rule attains the optimal leading term uniformly over the marginals. For every fixed positive definite Gaussian covariance, the same failure order holds, with a leading constant depending on the correlation matrix, and a rank-based rule attains the optimal leading failure probability without knowing the Gaussian parameters. In both models, we determine the optimal fixed cutoff and its leading failure constant; its failure probability exceeds the unrestricted optimum by a factor $Θ_d((\log\log n)^2)$. Under arbitrary dependence, a fixed joint density with uniform marginals can instead have optimal full-information success tending to approximately $0.58$. The proof uses the scarcity of observations with very small domination probability to bound every stopping rule. A matching rule selects a currently maximal point when this probability is below a threshold that increases as time runs out. Coordinate ranks from an initial sample provide sufficiently accurate estimates to preserve the optimal leading failure probability. For singular Gaussian distributions with known correlations, we characterize the optimal failure asymptotics attainable using ranks. Singular dependence can make every observation acceptable or recover the difficulty of selecting a single best point.

Title: At What Cost? (In)efficiency in First-Price Procurement Auctions
Authors: Simone Palazzotto, Andrés Cristi
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne
Abstract: We study the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions. We measure efficiency by the Price of Anarchy (PoA): the ratio between the expected social cost in equilibrium and the minimum expected social cost resulting from a socially optimal allocation. We first show that the standard first-price procurement auction has no bounded PoA guarantee. We construct equilibria in which every bidder is indifferent between all bids in a common interval, so that bids can be arbitrarily large, and the PoA is unbounded. If costs lie in an interval $[\underline c,\bar c]$ but bids are not restricted, the PoA equals the trivial ratio $\bar c/\underline c$. We hence study ways to restore a finite guarantee, first by characterizing the PoA when bids lie in $[\underline c,\bar c]$, which leads to the tight bound $1 + \frac1{e^2}(\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}-1)$. Alternatively, we introduce the notion of a phantom bidder: the auctioneer accepts the lowest bid only if it does not exceed a phantom bid, drawn independently of the costs, and otherwise buys from an outside option at cost $\bar c$. We show that a simple fixed phantom bid, i.e., a deterministic cap, gives PoA $=\frac1e\sqrt {\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}+O(1)$. We further show that no phantom mechanism whose construction depends only on the cost interval, under a mild regularity condition, whatever distribution it uses and whatever it reveals about the phantom bid before bidding, can improve on the $\sqrt{\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}$ dependence.

Title: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2
Authors: Andrés Cristi, J. Zhang
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne
Abstract: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size. We compute the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and show that a $1/2$ guarantee always holds with at most three buyers.

Title: Miscalibrated AI improves human calibration: An alignment problem for AI-assisted Decision education
Authors: Phillip Hegeman, Eeshan Hasan, Eungik Lee, Andrew Caplin, Jennifer S. Trueblood
Affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington; The Ohio State University; Federal Reserve Bank of New York; New York University
Abstract: Using artificial intelligence (AI) well requires probabilistic thinking, and central to it is calibration: expressing certainty that matches one's actual accuracy. Calibration is a decision skill, but a notoriously difficult one to teach. Because AI systems typically generate a probability alongside every prediction, observing these probabilities may help humans learn to provide better calibrated judgments. This is one form of what we call AI-assisted decision education -- using AI to teach the judgment skills that decision-making requires -- of which learning by observation, as here, is among the simplest forms. In a preregistered experiment, novice participants (N = 300) judged the probability that images of white blood cells were cancerous, before and after exposure to a highly accurate (94%) convolutional neural network. A single model was shown in three ways, holding accuracy fixed while varying the certainty it expressed: its original probabilities, which were conservative and poorly calibrated for the model's accuracy; a recalibrated version, well calibrated for the model and correspondingly certain; or categorical predictions carrying no probability information. When later tested without the AI, only the original, conservative display improved participants' calibration. It did so by reducing over-extremity, without a condition-specific improvement in discrimination. Notably, the display that taught best was the one miscalibrated for the model. AI-assisted decision education therefore faces an alignment problem: the signal that best describes a model, need not be the signal that best supports the learner.

Title: ASTOR: Benchmarking and Improving Autoformulation for Soft-Constraint Optimization with a Formal Grammar
Authors: Amer Goel, Yeganeh Alimohammadi, Andrew Daw
Abstract: Real-world decision problems combine two qualitatively different kinds of constraints: requirements that must be satisfied, called hard constraints, and preferences that can be violated, called soft constraints. Because these problems are often posed to decision-makers in natural language, large language models offer a natural tool for assisting with their solution. This has given rise to autoformulation, which focuses on using LLMs to translate natural-language descriptions of decision problems into executable mathematical optimization models. However, this research often neglects soft constraints like those proposed by consumers, managers, and planners, despite the fact that many practical problems require modeling them explicitly. We introduce ASTOR, an inference-time framework that maps a natural-language decision problem to a grammar-guided abstract syntax tree (AST) before deterministically compiling the resulting representation into executable optimization code. We also introduce SoftOR, a unified benchmark of natural language problems which focuses on soft constraint formulations. On SoftOR, ASTOR achieves the best aggregate accuracy among comparable single-request and multi-agent LLM methods while remaining competitive on standard autoformulation benchmarks that include only hard constraints. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/astor-softor-iclr-E34C/README.md.

Title: Monetary Policy in the Age of Universal Banking
Authors: Michael Gelman, Itay Goldstein, Andrew MacKinlay

Title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
Authors: Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
Affiliations: Santa Fe Institute; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.

Title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
Authors: Thomas Brennan, Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
Affiliations: Harvard University; Santa Fe Institute; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

Title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
Authors: Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
Affiliations: Santa Fe Institute; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

Title: Good human thinking populates AI's semantic blind spots
Authors: Kibum Moon, Dan Richard Johnson, Kostadin Kushlev, Oded Kleinmintz, Benjamín Lira, Indre Viskontas, James C. Kaufman, Roger E. Beaty, Nirav Patel, Emily Wenger, Angela Lee Duckworth, Adam E. Green

Abstract: AI-generated outputs tend to be more similar (homogenized) than human ideas. Does the human heterogeneity that extends beyond AI homogenization reflect valuable thinking that AI misses, or bad human ideas that AI avoids? We quantified how much an individual response expands an idea space beyond recurring clusters of ideas, enabling us to identify human responses located in AI's "semantic blind spots" (regions AI sparsely covers). Across three large samples (college admissions essays, alternative uses of objects, and interpersonal problem solving), human ideas in AI blind spots predicted higher academic achievement and performed as well or better on creativity, quality, and effectiveness. In contrast to humans, when AI expanded idea space, the association with creativity weakened or reversed. AI blind spots persisted across 66 diverse models and were not resolved by human-AI collaboration. Thinking "outside the bots" does not appear to reflect low-performing human variation that AI can safely omit.

Title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
Authors: Jun Li, Robert Bray, Sébastien Martin, Nils Van den Steen, Andrew Wu, Xiao Ni, Arielle Anderer, Ekaterina Astashkina, Владимир Бабич, Jean-Paul Baldwin, Hamsa Bastani, Christian Blanco, Oğuzhan Çelebi, Christopher Chen, Shi Chen, Benjamin C. Collier, Yao Cui, Pnina Feldman, Blair Flicker, Brian Han, Yichun Hu, Daniela Hurtado-Lange, Jane Jiang, Zhaohui Jiang, Ismail Kirci, Murat Köksalan, Zhen Lian, Hongyan Liang, Mengshi Lu, Lesley Meng, Ken Moon, Mi Kyong Newsom, Minje Park, Chris Parker, Anyan Qi, Meng Qi, Debjit Roy, Neha Sharma, Alp Sungu, Tom Tan, Necati Tereyağoğlu, Hanu Tyagi, Sriram Venkataraman, Guihua Wang, Yixin Wang, Owen Wu, Zonghao Yang, Qiuping Yu, Sophie Yu, Jingwei Zhang, Wenchang Zhang, Ruihao Zhu

Abstract: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

Title: Minimax-Optimal Static Estimators Under Interference
Authors: Arthur Delarue, Ilan Lobel
Affiliations: University of Virginia; New York University
Abstract: We study the problem of estimating the global treatment effect in randomized experiments under interference, where a unit's outcome may depend on the treatment assignments of other units. We adopt a minimax framework, allowing an adversary to select an outcome function from a class of functions that satisfy bounded outcomes and bounded interference. We derive minimax-optimal static estimators that are robust to a wide range of interference structures, parameterized by a scalar $δ$ controlling the maximum influence of one unit's treatment on another's outcome. Under large interference, we observe two regimes. When the treatment and control groups are equally sized, the minimax-optimal static estimator is the zero estimator. When one of the two groups is larger, the minimax-optimal static estimator is a "half-zero" estimator, in which the outcomes of the smaller group are ignored, and the estimator only considers the outcomes of the larger group.

Title: Calibrating LLM Tutor Initiation to Learner Expertise: Proactive and Reactive Support for Computational Thinking
Authors: Arun Rai, Liwei Chen, Balasubramaniam Ramesh, Cynthia Breazeal, Yuan Long, Benjamin Ampel, Andrea Aria

Title: Toward an AI-Powered Computational Testbed for Workforce Policy
Authors: Sumer Sumeet Vaid, Ashley V. Whillans
Affiliations: Harvard University
Abstract: Workforce transformations are difficult to forecast and costly to mismanage. In particular, the integration of artificial intelligence into knowledge work currently affects a substantial share of the global workforce, yet this transition proceeds without tools to forecast how individual employees will respond psychologically and behaviorally. We combine recent advances in LLM-powered generative agents with foundational management science and organizational behavior research to propose dynamic employee agents. Among consenting populations, these agents can be seeded with HR records, validated psychometric measures, and digital activity data to simulate employees' cognitive, emotional, and behavioral trajectories across successive workdays during planned organizational changes. In this article, we detail the computational architecture required to construct this simulation platform and define the privacy, accuracy, and representativeness safeguards necessary for responsible deployment. We argue that establishing this prospective forecasting infrastructure is a critical technical requirement for managing the current global workforce realignment around AI.

Title: Digital Fragmentation and Generative AI Use Across 103 Million Application Events
Authors: Sumer Sumeet Vaid, Ashley V. Whillans
Affiliations: Harvard University
Abstract: Knowledge workers switch between applications thousands of times per day, spending nearly a tenth of the work year transitioning between digital applications in a process called digital fragmentation. Whether this fragmentation reflects who an employee is, where they work, or what kind of day they are having, has remained an open question. We analyzed 103 million application events recorded second-by-second from 1,017 employees across eight organizations that largely employ knowledge workers (e.g., law, financial services). Day-to-day variation in fragmentation within individual employees accounted for 44.6% of the variation in digital fragmentation, slightly exceeding stable individual differences between employees (35.8%), and far exceeding variation between organizations (19.6%). Fragmentation rose over the work week and reset after weekends and holidays. Higher-than-typical use of communication applications coincided with more fragmented work. Generative AI use also occurred on more fragmented days, but the period following AI use was marked by narrower, longer, and more predictable application use. These findings identify the workday as a key level for understanding and intervening on digital fragmentation and suggest that AI may help structure fragmented work rather than merely intensify it.

Title: Benchmarking Psychological Dynamics in Generative Agents
Authors: Sumer Sumeet Vaid, Ashley V. Whillans
Affiliations: Harvard University
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to simulate human behavior, acting as computational replicas of human subjects. Yet the lived psychological experience of humans is difficult to benchmark, particularly as it unfolds over time. We introduce a psychometric benchmark for computational replicas: personas that carry a fixed identity through an evolving sequence of events. Built entirely from published norms and meta-analytic effects, the benchmark scores two dimensions of psychological realism. The first, internal validity, quantifies whether generated trajectories reproduce the internal structure of repeated human measurement: distributions, the between- versus within-person variance partition, temporal dependence, and range. The second, external validity, quantifies whether replicas recover established trait, state, and indicator relations. Across 36 open-weight and proprietary LLMs from nine developers (1B-671B parameters), most recover the direction of established relations (84.3% mean agreement) and the variance partition (26 of 34), yet the within-person correlation and distributional structure elude recovery. Internal validity is independent of scale and capability: a mid-size open LLM (Gemma-3-27B) strikes the best trade-off between the two dimensions. The benchmark is a precondition for using computational replicas in causal inference across domains (e.g., marketing, healthcare), and identifies within-person grounding as the central challenge ahead.

Title: Efficient Interview Scheduling for Stable Matching
Authors: Moshe Babaioff, Rotem Gil, Assaf Romm
Affiliations: Hebrew University of Jerusalem
Abstract: The study of stable matchings usually relies on the assumption that agents' preferences over the opposite side are complete and known. In many real markets, however, preferences might be uncertain and revealed only through costly interactions such as interviews. We show how to reach interim-stable matchings, under which all matched pairs must have interviewed and agents use expected utilities whenever true values remain unknown, while minimizing both the expected number of interviews and the expected number of interview rounds. We introduce two adaptive algorithms that produce interim-stable matchings: one operates sequentially, and another is a hybrid algorithm that begins by scheduling some interviews in parallel and continues sequentially. Focusing on cases where agents are ex-ante indifferent between agents on the other side, we show that the sequential algorithm performs 2 interviews per agent in expectation. We complement this by showing that any algorithm that performs less than 2 interviews per agent, does not always guarantee interim-stability. We also demonstrate that the hybrid algorithm requires only polylogarithmic expected number of rounds, while still performing only about 2 interviews per agent in expectation. Additionally, the interviews scheduled by our algorithms guarantee an interim-stable matching when Deferred-Acceptance is run after all interviews are completed.

Title: Variance-Adaptive Optimal Algorithm for Reinforcement Learning with Multinomial Logit Function Approximation
Authors: Wonyoung Kim, Min-Hwan Oh, Garud Iyengar, Assaf J. Zeevi
Affiliations: Seoul National University; Columbia University
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with multinomial logistic (MNL) function approximation has become an important framework due to its flexibility and broad applicability. While existing studies have established regret guarantees under worst-case analysis, they do not capture how performance depends on the variability of the interaction between the learner and the environment. In this paper, we develop a new theoretical analysis for MNL-based Markov decision processes that yields explicit variance-adaptive regret bounds. Our algorithm is computationally efficient and achieves the instance-wise optimal rate of regret, narrowing the gap between upper and lower bounds. Our numerical experiments validate that our method learns optimal policies more efficiently than conventional approaches.

Title: Oblivious Learning and Collusive Pricing
Authors: Yuhang Wu, Assaf J. Zeevi
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: On a platform with many sellers, should a pricing algorithm explicitly model competitors' prices when learning demand? Classical arguments suggest that ignoring competitors induces model misspecification and inefficiency, yet findings from algorithmic collusion suggest that ignoring competitor prices may, surprisingly, facilitate collusive outcomes and improve profits. We study this problem in a competitive market with unknown noisy demand, in which sellers repeatedly set prices, either incorporating competitor prices in learning their demand models (informed), or ignoring them (oblivious). We show that, relative to a monopolist, an oblivious seller in a competitive market must conduct more aggressive price exploration to compensate for the loss of dynamic competitor information. When all sellers are oblivious, prices converge to the competitive outcome under persistent exploration, while a continuum of pseudo-equilibria arises when exploration is "insufficient." In markets with a mix of oblivious and informed sellers, the informed strictly out-earn the oblivious. In game-theoretic terms, the unique Nash equilibrium is the all-informed market, in which prices converge to the competitive outcome efficiently, and oblivious modeling does not robustly lead to collusive patterns.
